Mr Weston, who loved company above all things, invited the whole neighbourhood to a Christmas Eve dinner at Randalls, and nothing would persuade him to take a refusal. Mr Woodhouse hesitated and fretted, for he disliked cold, dark roads and strange tables, but Isabella and Emma coaxed him until at last he gave way. The household began to prepare for the first great evening of the Christmas season.

Harriet's cold had grown worse, so that she could not possibly go to Randalls, and Emma stopped at the school to console her with a kiss and a promise to tell her everything. At the party Mr Elton, in remarkably high spirits, asked in a loud voice for news of Harriet and then fell silent about her entirely. Emma, who was busy congratulating herself, put the strange cheerfulness down to the pleasures of Christmas.

Over dinner Mr John Knightley, who had nothing to do but watch, saw plainly that Mr Elton's smiles were for Emma and not for Harriet. When the guests had a quiet moment together, he told her gently that the vicar seemed to be in love with her, and he advised her to look about her. Emma laughed with the confidence of a woman who is certain she knows better, and assured him that Mr Elton was in love with Harriet.

While the guests were drinking tea, someone noticed that snow had begun to fall thickly, and by the time the curtains were drawn back the ground was already white. Mr Weston, always cheerful, said that the carriages could easily get home, but Mr Woodhouse wrung his hands and begged that they should start at once. The ladies, who could hear the wind rising in the chimneys, were suddenly very eager to be safe at home before the roads grew worse.

Mr Elton, who had taken a good deal of wine, was in a state of excited and rather alarming gaiety, and when the carriages were called he contrived to place himself in Emma's. The door closed, the horses started, and she found herself alone with him in the dark, with only the lamps and the falling snow for company. She could think of nothing to say, and he, unfortunately, could think of a great deal.

Mr Elton, without warning or ceremony, seized Emma's hand and began to pour out a stream of passionate words, declaring that he adored her and had lived only for her smiles. Emma, who had never imagined such a thing, drew back in horror and for a moment could not speak at all. The carriage rolled on through the snow, and the whole beautiful plan of her winter fell silently to pieces.

Emma recovered her voice enough to tell him that he had mistaken her entirely, and that she had believed all his attentions to be meant for her friend Harriet. Mr Elton, who had never thought of Harriet except as a poor girl of no family, replied with offended pride that he had never cared a straw for her. They finished the journey in a silence so cold that the snow outside seemed warm by comparison.

Safe at last in her own room, Emma sat down and went over the whole winter in her mind, and with every memory the truth grew clearer. Mr Elton's praise, his glances, his visits and his charade had all been meant for her, and she had pushed poor Harriet, in all her innocence, straight into a bitter disappointment. Never in all her twenty years had she felt so deeply ashamed of her own cleverness, or so little able to take pride in it.

Emma lay awake for most of the night, while the candle burned lower and the wind sighed in the chimney. She blamed herself severely for her vanity, her blindness and her foolish confidence, and the memory of Mr Knightley's warning stung her like a nettle. By morning she had made a solemn resolution never again to play with other people's hearts, though the future would test it more than once.

In the morning the snow lay deep over Hartfield, and the roads were so blocked that no one could possibly go out. Emma, who was torn between dread and duty, was secretly glad of the delay, for she did not know how she could bear to tell Harriet what she had to say. Her father, who guessed nothing, spent the morning at the window, announcing sadly how very cold it was.

As soon as the roads were passable, Emma hurried to Mrs Goddard's and told Harriet the truth as gently as she knew how, though no gentleness could make it any less cruel. Harriet, who had begun to believe in her own happiness, wept on the sofa with her face hidden in a shawl, while Emma held her hand and accused herself of every fault. It was a bitter hour for both of them, and neither of the two friends was ever to forget the sorrow of that grey morning.

Mr Elton, whose vanity had been wounded to the quick, did not wait to be laughed at by the neighbours, and soon left Highbury for Bath, where he planned to remain for some weeks. Emma, who dreaded nothing so much as meeting him in the village, was thankful to hear of his departure. She only hoped that he would be gone long enough for Harriet's heart to mend.

When the Christmas visit was over, Isabella packed her five children into the carriage and returned to London, while Mr Woodhouse stood at the door complaining of the sudden quiet. Before leaving, Mr John Knightley took Emma aside and told her, with surprising kindness, that she would do well to stop meddling in the affairs of the heart. Emma, who had no reply to make, only blushed and promised to remember it.

Determined to make amends, Emma invited Harriet to Hartfield almost every day, and she read aloud to her while Harriet sat sewing quietly by the window. She chose sensible books and cheerful talk, and she tried to turn her friend's thoughts toward the kind of simple, solid happiness that does not depend on a vicar. It was a slow cure, but Harriet, who was too gentle to hold a grudge, did slowly begin to smile again.

One evening, when her father had gone early to bed, Emma sat alone with an unfinished drawing in her lap and thought of all that had happened. She promised herself, very seriously, that she would never again arrange anyone's marriage, and she meant it with her whole heart. Whether a heart so young and so fond of its own opinions could really keep such a promise was another question altogether.

The winter passed away in quiet routine, with long evenings at Hartfield, small dinners and a good deal of gossip, and by degrees Harriet's face lost its look of grief. When the first buds showed on the trees outside Emma's window, it seemed that the whole sorry story of Mr Elton had been folded away like a winter coat. Highbury, which had no great tragedies of its own, returned contentedly to its small affairs.

All Highbury had long waited for the arrival of Frank Churchill, the son of Mr Weston by his first wife, who had been adopted by a rich aunt and uncle in Yorkshire. Each time he promised to come, some excuse arrived from his aunt, whose health and humours governed the whole family's plans. Mr Weston, who loved his son, read each new letter aloud with hope and then, with a sigh, put it away again.

Beside the Randalls fire, Mr Weston spoke proudly of his son, who had been taken as a small child into the care of his mother's rich relations after her early death. The Churchills, who had no children of their own, had brought him up as their heir, and he had taken their name. Mr Weston, who could not have afforded such an education himself, admitted that the arrangement was a good one, though it cost him his son's company.

Mr Knightley declared on the lawn that a young man who truly wished to see his father would find a way to do so, whatever his aunt might say. Emma, who was curious about the unknown Frank and always ready to argue, replied that people who live under another person's roof cannot always do as they please. Neither would give way, and they parted with the polite hostility of two friends who each believe the other quite wrong.

Once again the longed-for visit was postponed, and Mrs Weston, who had hoped to please her husband, watched the empty road from her window with a sigh. Mrs Churchill had been taken ill, as she so often was, and her nephew could not possibly leave her side. Mr Weston hid his disappointment bravely, but his wife noticed that he spoke of the weather a good deal more than usual.

Miss Bates arrived at Hartfield one morning in great haste, with her bonnet crooked and a letter fluttering in her hand, to announce the most delightful news. Her niece, Jane Fairfax, was coming to stay in Highbury for a long visit, and the whole neighbourhood must hear of it at once. She was so happy that she forgot to sit down, and so talkative that Emma had difficulty in finding a gap in which to say that she was glad.

Miss Bates read out parts of the letter with her glasses on the end of her nose, interrupting herself every few lines to add a remark of her own. Jane, she explained, had lost both her parents when she was very small, and Colonel Campbell, an old friend of her father's, had taken her into his family and given her the best of educations. Now that the Campbells were going away to Ireland, Jane would spend some months in Highbury before earning her living as a governess.

Miss Bates, who could never speak of anyone without praising him, declared that Mr Knightley was the kindest of neighbours, since he had sent her and her mother almost all of his apples, leaving none for himself. Mrs Bates was old and deaf, the family was poor, and such quiet gifts, given without any fuss, meant more than she could say. Emma, who knew his habits, was not surprised, but she felt a small glow of pride in her friend.

Jane Fairfax stepped down from the carriage at the Bateses' door, tall and graceful, with dark eyelashes, a fine complexion and a manner of perfect calm. She was accomplished at the piano and at everything else she had been taught, and all Highbury soon agreed that she was a model of elegance. Emma, who ought to have been delighted to meet such a girl, could not for the life of her feel any warmth.

Emma made an effort to be agreeable, and she asked Jane a number of questions about Weymouth, about Ireland and above all about the handsome Mr Dixon, whom the Campbells' daughter had married. Jane replied to everything with a calm and careful politeness that revealed nothing, and when she was asked whether Mr Dixon was really so charming, she answered that most people thought so. Emma, who dearly loved to hear a good story and was seldom denied one, found her quite unbearably reserved.

Mr Knightley, standing at the window while a cart rumbled by, remarked that Emma was hard on Jane Fairfax, and that he suspected the reason. Jane, he said, was exactly the quiet, studious and accomplished girl whom Emma's friends had always held up as a model, and nobody likes a model. Emma blushed and changed the subject, but his words stayed with her, as unwelcome truths so often do.

One bright morning Mr Weston hurried into Hartfield, so full of joy that he could hardly speak in whole sentences. His son had arrived two days earlier than anyone expected, and, as he declared to the astonished company, the young man was already on his way to pay his respects. Emma, who had heard so much of Frank Churchill, felt her curiosity rise to the highest point.

Frank Churchill bowed gracefully as he entered the drawing room, a handsome, slender young man with a ready smile and an air of easy good manners. Within ten minutes he had charmed Mr Woodhouse by his gentle voice, amused Emma by his quick wit and managed to praise every object in the room. Emma, who had expected to meet a lazy, spoilt young man with too much money and too little purpose, found herself very pleasantly mistaken.

Frank asked Emma to show him the whole of Highbury, and they walked together down the high street, past the Crown Inn, the church and the busy shop at Ford's. He praised everything he saw, from the little ballroom above the inn to the crooked chimneys of the cottages, with a warmth that made the village seem rather grander than it was. Emma, who was not at all accustomed to so eager and appreciative a visitor, enjoyed herself far more than she had expected to do.

Frank, saying that he must pay his respects to an old friend of his father's family, knocked at the door of the Bateses' small house, and Emma waited in the street while he stayed rather longer than good manners required. She took it as a sign of a generous heart that he should be so attentive to poor Miss Bates and her mother. It did not occur to her to ask whom he had really come to see.

That night Emma sat at her desk and asked herself seriously whether she was falling in love with Frank Churchill, for he was handsome, amusing and clearly pleased with her company. She decided, after some thought, that she could not be certain, since her heart was not beating in the manner of heroines in novels. She resolved, being a sensible young woman in most matters except those of the heart, to wait and see what the next few weeks would show.

To the great surprise of the neighbourhood, Frank rode off to London one morning and came back with a newly cut head of hair, which, it appeared, had been the whole object of his journey. Mr Weston laughed it off as the harmless vanity of youth, and the ladies of Highbury declared it very charming, but there were some who thought it silly. Mr Knightley, hearing of it, said nothing at all, which was a bad sign.

When Mrs Weston spoke warmly of Frank's lively spirits, Mr Knightley frowned and said that a young man who crossed the country merely to have his hair cut was a trifler, vain and of no great seriousness. Emma, who was now quite prepared to defend Frank to the end, replied that high spirits were no crime and that Mr Knightley was too stern. The quarrel was a mild one, but it left both of them rather stiff.

At the Hartfield tea table, Frank set himself to please Mr Woodhouse, and it must be said that he did it admirably. He asked after the old gentleman's health with real attention, agreed that a good fire was one of life's great blessings and spoke in the gentlest voice of the dangers of night air. Mr Woodhouse, who valued kindness above wit, declared that he had never met a more thoughtful young man.

During a walk in the grounds at Randalls, Emma admitted to Frank that she had never been able to warm to Jane Fairfax, who was so correct and so reserved. Frank agreed readily that Miss Fairfax was a cold sort of girl, though he said it in a tone that was oddly light and careless. Emma, who was pleased to find her own opinion shared, never stopped to wonder why he spoke with such deliberate ease.

Mrs Weston, who loved both of them, watched Emma and Frank laughing together across the room, and in her kind heart she began to hope for a match. Emma, who understood her look perfectly well, was secretly amused and a little pleased, for there are few girls who dislike being thought of as a good wife for a handsome young man. She told herself, however, that she was not going to be hurried into love by anybody's hopes.

One morning a beautiful piano arrived at the Bateses' small house, and the two men who carried it into the tiny sitting room had to turn it this way and that to fit it through the door. No note came with it, no name was given, and Jane, who stood and stared at it with an unreadable face, declared that she did not know who could have sent such a gift. Within the hour the news had run from one end of Highbury to the other, and for days afterwards the village could speak of nothing else.

Miss Bates, who was delighted beyond measure, chattered to every visitor about the kindness of Colonel Campbell, who must have sent the piano from a distance to make the dear girl's stay more pleasant. Jane, however, stood by the instrument with a deep blush and said almost nothing, and she seemed more troubled than glad. Emma noticed this at once, and, being a young woman who delighted in a mystery, she thought it very curious indeed.

Emma, who loved a mystery, whispered to Frank that the piano had probably been sent not by Colonel Campbell but by Mr Dixon, the Campbells' handsome and married son-in-law. Frank listened with a delighted air, agreed that it was exactly what a man in love would do, and asked a great many eager questions. Emma took his interest as a sign of kindred minds, and was happier than she had been for weeks.

That evening, standing at her window, Emma looked toward the Bateses' house and built up a complete romance in her head. Jane, she decided, had fallen in love with Mr Dixon, who had married her friend Miss Campbell instead, and he, filled with remorse, had sent the instrument as a secret token of regret. It was a very satisfying story, and its only fault was that there was not a word of truth in it.

Mrs Weston, who had her own ideas, gently suggested in a quiet corner that the piano might have been a gift from Mr Knightley, who was fond of Jane and of music. Emma was truly alarmed and cried that he must never think of marrying anybody, since his nephew Henry was to have Donwell and she would not have him cheated of it. Mrs Weston said nothing more, but she looked at Emma with a thoughtful smile.

The Coles, who had risen from trade to considerable wealth, had lately taken to entertaining on a larger scale, and Emma, who valued rank above riches, had always meant to refuse their invitations. When she learned that Mr Weston, Mr Knightley and all the neighbours had been asked and that no card had come for Hartfield, she was surprised to find herself rather hurt. It was a useful lesson in how much one's pride depends on being asked.

The invitation came at last, a day later than the others, and Emma, who had decided that kindness was better than pride, accepted it with a gracious smile. She arrived at the Coles' bright drawing room in a pale gown, was treated like a queen by her hosts and found, with some surprise, that their dinner was both handsome and cheerful. It was quite impossible, she found, to remain superior for long in such a generous and cheerful atmosphere as theirs.

When the ladies and gentlemen came together after dinner, Jane was begged to play, and she sat down at the Coles' handsome new instrument and played with a delicacy that silenced the whole room. Frank, who had a pleasant voice, joined her in a song, and the two of them performed together with a certainty that surprised even Emma. She thought it a pleasant duet between two good singers, and nothing more than that, which was precisely where she made her mistake.

Mr Knightley, who had taken no part in the music, stood a little apart with his eyes fixed upon the singers, and Emma, joining him, could not help noticing his serious face. He remarked quietly that Miss Fairfax looked exhausted, and that it was unkind to ask a girl who was not strong to perform for so long. Emma, who disliked being told what to see, replied lightly that it was only a song, and he made no answer.

The carriages rolled away in the starry dark, and Emma, wrapped in her shawl, drove home with the comfortable feeling of an evening well spent. She had enjoyed the company, admired the music and, as she thought, penetrated the whole secret of the piano, so that she went to bed in a most agreeable humour. She would have gone to bed a good deal less cheerfully, and have slept a good deal less soundly, had she known how entirely wrong she was.

Mr Weston, who could never resist a party, and Frank, who loved dancing, decided to hold a ball at the Crown Inn. They led Emma from corner to corner of the great room while they argued about how many couples it would hold, and the idea spread through Highbury like fire through dry leaves. Soon the young people could talk of nothing but dresses, partners and music, and Emma, who loved dancing as much as anyone, gave her opinion on everything and was very happy.

Emma and Mrs Weston sat down at a table covered with paper and drew up a list of guests, which they altered and corrected a dozen times. They wanted about thirty people, enough to fill the room without crowding, all of them respectable, cheerful and able to dance. It was a pleasant task, for each name brought a picture of how the evening might go.

Mr Woodhouse, hearing of the ball, frowned and rubbed his hands and declared that dancing in a crowded room was the surest way to catch a cold. Emma, who knew how to manage him, soothed his fears with gentle jokes, promised him a very warm shawl and reminded him that Mr Perry would certainly be near at hand. By evening the old man was almost reconciled, though he still hoped the whole thing might be forgotten.

A letter arrived from Enscombe while the party at Randalls were at breakfast, and Frank turned pale as he read it, for Mrs Churchill had been taken ill and demanded her nephew's return. He knew that there was no appeal against the summons, for his aunt had a way of becoming ill precisely when he wished to be happy. Mr Weston, white with disappointment, could only shake his head and say that it was a very great pity, and that nothing could be done.

Frank came to Hartfield to say goodbye, and Emma noticed that he seemed unable to leave, standing at the door with his hat in his hand and a look of real distress. He said a great deal about how sorry he was to leave Highbury, and a little, in a lower voice, about how sorry he was to leave her. Emma was quite sure that he was on the point of declaring something, but at the last moment he bowed and was gone.

Alone in her room that evening, Emma examined her feelings as thoroughly as a scientist examines a puzzling specimen. She missed Frank's company, and she thought of him often, but she could not discover in herself the burning passion that a true heroine should feel. She therefore concluded that she was not in love after all, and she resolved to be cheerful for the sake of everyone around her.

The ball was given up, and the great room at the Crown, which had been swept, polished and hung with candles in the minds of half Highbury, stood dark and empty under its dust sheets. Mr Weston, who had looked forward to it more than anyone, bore the loss with good humour, but the young people of the village felt that a real pleasure had been snatched from them. Emma, who had planned her dress, could not help wishing that Mrs Churchill's illnesses were less convenient.

On a rainy morning Emma sat in the window seat reading a letter from Mrs Weston, which said that Mrs Churchill's illness had proved a long one. Frank could not leave Enscombe for weeks, and perhaps for months, and the Westons were resigned to waiting. Emma, who found the news disappointing, was obliged to admit that she missed him more than a girl who was not in love ought to do.

News ran through Highbury that Mr Elton, after so short a stay in Bath, was returning with a bride, and every window was alive with speculation. It was said that she was rich, that she was handsome and that her name was Miss Augusta Hawkins, but nobody could say more. Emma, who remembered the vicar's words in the carriage, could not help feeling that he had been remarkably quick to console himself.

Emma hurried to Mrs Goddard's, fearing that the news would open Harriet's wound, and found her looking out of the window with a thoughtful face. To her surprise Harriet said that she was a good deal better, that she wished Mr Elton every happiness and that she hoped never to be so foolish again. Emma squeezed her hand, relieved, though she suspected that the bravery might not last.

Mr Elton returned with his bride, Augusta Hawkins, a lady who was rich, handsome in her own opinion and exceedingly pleased with her new position. He introduced her proudly to the neighbours in a Highbury parlour, and the two of them smiled so widely that Emma half expected their faces to split. Emma, who disliked her at first sight and could not have said exactly why, was polite, as the occasion required.

Mrs Elton spoke endlessly of her brother-in-law's great house, Maple Grove, which, it seemed, surpassed everything that Surrey could boast of, from its trees to its carriages. She mentioned its barouche-landau so often that Emma began to dream about it, and she treated Emma throughout as a promising young lady rather than as the first lady in Highbury. Emma bore the whole account with a fixed smile, a polite murmur from time to time and a rapidly growing headache.

Mrs Elton, who had no idea of the proper way to address a gentleman she scarcely knew, called Mr Knightley simply Knightley, as if he were her cousin or her servant. Mr Knightley, who had been Mr Knightley to everyone for thirty years, stiffened a little and looked at Emma with eyes that were quietly amused. Emma, who nearly laughed aloud, felt for the first time that she and he were on the same side.

Mrs Elton took it upon herself to organise the society of Highbury, which she did with an air of conferring a favour, and she referred to her husband on every possible occasion as her caro sposo. She planned to start a music club, to give advice on housekeeping and to introduce Emma to all the people that Emma had known since she was a baby. Emma, who had always been first in Highbury, found it very hard to be gracious.

Mrs Elton took Jane Fairfax under her wing with a great show of kindness, and in the Bateses' parlour she offered to find her an excellent position as a governess. Jane thanked her with cool politeness and said that she was not yet ready to think of leaving, but Mrs Elton, who did not take hints, repeated the offer every time they met. Poor Miss Bates, who was proud of both of them, did not know where to look.

At a small gathering in the village, Mr Elton looked coldly past Harriet as though she were a piece of furniture, and he turned to speak to someone else the moment she approached. Harriet bit her lip and said nothing, but Emma, who saw the whole thing, felt a hot wave of anger rise in her cheeks. It was one thing to refuse a girl, and quite another to wound her in public.

One evening Frank rode into the yard of the Crown Inn, tired and dusty from his long journey, for Mrs Churchill had recovered and had let him go. Mr Weston, who was waiting at the door, embraced him with a happiness so complete that half the street came to its windows. Emma, who heard the news at breakfast the next morning, was surprised by how glad she was and rather puzzled to find it so.

Jane, who was growing paler with every week, refused another of Mrs Elton's invitations, and she did so with such quiet firmness that nothing could be said. Mrs Elton, who could not understand why anyone should decline her favour, told all her friends that Jane was proud and secretive and not at all what she appeared. Emma, who was beginning to see that Jane's reserve might hide something besides coldness, was not so sure.

Frank called at Hartfield the next morning, and Emma greeted him warmly in the hall, glad to see a face that was not Mrs Elton's. He was as charming as ever, but she thought that he seemed a little quieter, as if something weighed on his mind. She attributed this to anxiety about his aunt, which was kind of her, though not quite correct.

Mr Weston, waving a paper triumphantly in the hall of Randalls, announced that the ball was to go forward at last, since Mrs Churchill was well and Frank was free of his duties. The date was fixed, the Crown was engaged and the music was promised, and the whole village burst into a happy flutter of preparation. Even Mr Woodhouse, to everyone's surprise, was heard to say that perhaps one night's dancing would not kill anybody.

The long-awaited evening arrived at last, and the great room at the Crown, hung with candles and garlands, filled gradually with all the beauty and fashion of Highbury. The musicians tuned their instruments, the young people took their places along the walls, and a happy murmur of anticipation rose to the ceiling. Even those who would have been quite content to stay at home found themselves tapping their feet.

Emma arrived at the Crown with the Westons, wearing her best white gown, and she was pleased to see the admiration in several pairs of eyes. Frank hurried forward to greet her, bowed with all his usual grace and begged to be allowed the first dance. It was one of those moments when everything seems to be going exactly as it should, which is rarely a good sign.

Mrs Elton swept into the ballroom in white lace and a necklace of pearls, with the air of a queen opening a new bridge, and her husband followed at her elbow in a proud glow of satisfaction. She took a seat in the middle of the room, where everyone could admire her, and she began at once to criticise the candles, the floor and the music. Emma, who was standing across the room with the Westons, composed her features into an expression of polite and perfect blankness.

Mr Knightley, who disliked dancing less than he pretended but did not often indulge in it, stood by the wall with his hands behind his back, watching the couples with a thoughtful eye. Emma noticed that he looked taller, firmer and more distinguished than any of the young men who were hopping about the floor. She put the thought away at once, as one puts away a coat for which one has no use.

Harriet, who had been promised a partner by half the neighbourhood, stood at the side of the room in her prettiest dress, hoping to be asked to dance. Mr Elton, who happened to be close by, was begged by a friend to take her hand, and he refused so loudly and so rudely that everyone nearby fell silent. She went quite pale, and her face drooped like a flower in a frost.

Mrs Elton, who had understood the situation at once, joined her husband in cutting Harriet as pointedly as she could, and the two of them exchanged a smiling glance that made Emma's blood boil. Harriet, standing alone and humiliated, kept her eyes on the floor and tried not to cry. Emma, who longed to rescue her but could think of no way to do it, burned with anger.

Then Mr Knightley, who had seen everything, walked across the room, bowed to Harriet and offered his hand with the calm, grave courtesy of a man who has never in his life been afraid of public opinion. Harriet, astonished and very grateful, rose from her seat, and a faint colour returned to her cheeks as they took their places in the dance. Emma, who was watching from the other side of the room with her heart beating fast, could have embraced him there and then in front of everyone.

When the dance ended, Emma crossed to Mr Knightley and thanked him first with her eyes and then with her words, adding that Mr Elton had behaved like a brute. Mr Knightley replied that Mr Elton had meant to be cruel, and that it had been a pleasure to disappoint him, and his whole face broke into the smile that she liked best. Emma, suddenly aware that they had been quarrelling a great deal lately, felt that it was a very good moment to make peace.

Later in the evening Emma, who had no partner, asked Mr Knightley with a laugh whether he would dance with her, since they were so nearly brother and sister that it could not be improper. Mr Knightley answered, rather quickly, that they were certainly not brother and sister, and he led her out with a peculiar look on his face. Emma could not tell what it meant, and she was too happy to ask.

Frank had danced with Emma and then with Jane, and Emma, glancing across at the supper table, noticed that the two of them were speaking together in low voices with an unusual earnestness. She thought nothing of it, supposing that it was kindness toward a lonely girl. The last dance ended, the carriages came, and the guests drifted out into the night with glowing faces.

The next day Harriet, walking on a quiet lane with a school friend, was surrounded by a crowd of begging children and a few rough, shouting strangers, who would not let her pass. Her friend ran ahead to look for help, and Harriet was left alone, shaking, with a pocket full of coins and no idea what to do. It was, she afterwards declared, the most frightening quarter of an hour of her whole short life, and she never entirely forgot it.

Frank, who was riding down the lane at that moment, took in the situation at a glance, scattered the beggars with a few firm words and dismounted to offer his arm. Harriet, trembling and half in tears, was led slowly toward Hartfield, where she arrived feeling that she had been rescued by a hero in a story. He, for his part, behaved as modestly as if he had done nothing at all, and he asked only that she should lean on him.

Harriet sat in Emma's drawing room with a glass of water in her hand and told the whole story in breathless fragments, while Emma listened with wide eyes. A lovely girl, a handsome young man, a sudden danger and a gallant rescue: it was exactly the sort of event that is supposed to begin a love story. Emma, who had promised herself never to make a match again, felt her promise melt like snow in the sun.

Frank stayed at Hartfield until Harriet was calm, and Emma, sitting between them, could not help noticing how well the handsome rescuer and the lovely rescued looked together. In her imagination she saw a small, bright wedding and herself in the front pew, smiling. She had promised not to make matches, but there is a difference, she told herself, between making a match and merely noticing one.

Mr Woodhouse, when he heard what had happened, wrung his hands and declared that the lanes of Surrey had never been so dangerous, and that nobody should walk anywhere without a servant. Emma soothed him by saying that the strangers had moved on by evening and that Highbury was quiet again. Mr Woodhouse was not convinced, but he allowed himself to be given a cup of tea.

Some days later Harriet, sitting in Emma's sitting room with a deep blush, confided that she had begun to care for a man who was a great deal above Mr Elton in every way. Emma, who was convinced that she knew exactly whom her friend meant, smiled and said nothing, since she had firmly resolved not to meddle. Saying nothing was, in her view, the highest form of delicacy, and she was proud of it.

Emma could not keep her pleasant thoughts to herself, and she hinted to Mrs Weston that Frank and Harriet seemed likely to become good friends, and perhaps something more. Mrs Weston, who had always hoped that Frank would choose Emma, looked puzzled and a little disappointed, and she remarked that Frank had never seemed to prefer any lady in particular. Emma only laughed and said that she was sure to be proved right in the end.

One morning Harriet came to Hartfield with a small wooden box in her hands, and she opened it with the air of a person who is about to make a great confession. Inside lay two humble keepsakes that Mr Elton had once handled, a scrap of sticking plaster and the end of an old pencil, which she had treasured for months in the foolishness of her first love. She said that she wished Emma to witness what she was going to do with them.

Harriet dropped the two little treasures into the grate, and the friends watched in silence as the plaster curled and the pencil blackened and the foolish romance of the winter turned to smoke. Harriet said, with a calm that surprised Emma, that she had learned her lesson and that she would never again attach herself to a man simply because he was kind. Emma, who had been prepared for tears, was moved to find that her friend was growing up.

That evening Emma sat at the piano and played while Harriet, who had a sweet voice, sang softly beside her, and nothing in Hartfield seemed amiss. Emma was convinced that her friend's cheerfulness could only be explained by a hopeful new attachment, and she asked no questions, which she considered the proof of her wisdom. The truth, as she was very shortly to learn, was a great deal stranger and a great deal more surprising than she supposed.

One wet afternoon at Hartfield, Frank produced a box of wooden letters of the kind used for teaching children their alphabet, and he proposed a game in which each person should spell out words for the others to guess. The company gathered round the table, Mr Woodhouse sat peacefully by the fire and, for a while, nothing was heard but laughter and the clicking of the letters. It seemed to everyone present a perfectly innocent amusement, and not one of them guessed what trouble the little wooden letters were about to cause.

Frank, with a mischievous smile, arranged a handful of letters to spell the name Dixon and pushed them across the table toward Jane Fairfax. Jane, who had been quietly enjoying herself, glanced at the word, and a deep flush spread across her face from her throat to her forehead. Emma, who thought she understood the joke perfectly, laughed with the rest and felt very clever.

Jane swept the letters away with a gesture that was almost angry, and then, as if she were ashamed of her temper, she recovered her calm and turned her face to the window. Emma, who was enjoying herself, supposed that Jane was embarrassed to have her secret exposed, and she gave Frank a conspiratorial smile. Frank, however, looked rather uncomfortable for a moment, and then he smiled again as though nothing whatever had happened between them.

Later, beside the garden wall, Mr Knightley spoke to Emma in a low voice, saying that he had seen a look pass between Frank and Jane and that he suspected that there was something between them. Emma, who was perfectly sure that Jane had no interest in Frank and that Frank had none in Jane, laughed at him kindly and told him that he was imagining things. Mr Knightley looked at her gravely and said that he hoped she was right, and then he said no more.

Every morning, without fail, Jane Fairfax walked down to the post office in Highbury, whatever the weather, and one day she was seen to return wet through, with a pale face and a letter in her hand. The village wondered why she was so eager, since her friends in Ireland could not possibly write so often, and Mr Knightley, who noticed such things, noticed this. Emma noticed it too, but she put it down to the romantic influence of Mr Dixon and the letters that came from Ireland.

Mrs Elton, who believed that she was the proper person to look after everyone, announced to Jane that she would send her own servant to collect the letters from the post office and spare Jane the trouble. Jane thanked her with great firmness and said that she needed the exercise, and that she preferred to fetch them herself. Mrs Elton shook a playful finger, but it was obvious that she was both surprised and annoyed.

Mrs Elton, who had never seen Donwell Abbey but was convinced that she knew how it should be used, proposed to Mr Knightley a grand picnic in the grounds. She wanted cold food under the trees, donkeys to ride and herself as the chief organiser, and she waved her hands as she told him exactly how he ought to host the day. Mr Knightley, who disliked fuss, listened with a stiff face and a long silence.

Mr Knightley replied, with great politeness and no flexibility at all, that he would not be organised by anybody. He intended to invite his friends to pick strawberries at Donwell on a fine day, as had been done for years, and there would be no donkeys, no fuss and no Mrs Elton in command. Mrs Elton, rather offended, declared that Mr Knightley was a very odd person, but she accepted the invitation.

Mr Woodhouse, who had not paid a visit to Donwell Abbey for years, sat comfortably in his chair and listened to Emma's account of the plan with a worried frown. After a long debate with himself, he agreed to go, on the strict condition that there should be a fire in the room where he was to sit, and that the windows should be kept shut. Emma assured him that Mr Knightley, who knew his habits, would see to everything.

On the morning of the party Emma packed a basket, put on a straw hat and glanced at the Hartfield clock with the pleasure of a child going on a holiday. It was the first truly warm day of summer, the sky was a clear blue and the whole neighbourhood seemed to have thrown off its winter cares. She had not the faintest idea, as she stepped into the carriage, that the day would hold a good deal more than strawberries.

On a warm June day the neighbours drove to Donwell Abbey to pick strawberries, and the beds, rich and red beneath their leaves, were soon the centre of a happy crowd. Mr Knightley moved among his guests with quiet hospitality, pointing out the best fruit and hiding his amusement at the clumsy efforts of the visitors. Mrs Elton, however, complained of the heat at once and gave advice on the garden that nobody had asked for.

Emma walked away from the crowd along the shady lime walk, admiring the old stone of the Abbey, the sheltered gardens and the green meadows beyond. She thought that she had never seen a place so perfectly English or so quietly honourable, and the house seemed to her like its master, solid, kind and without display. She was surprised to find how much pleasure the thought gave her, and how long she lingered over it.

Mrs Elton, in a straw hat decorated with ribbons and carrying a very pretty basket, picked strawberries with such energy that she soon had more than anyone, and she told everybody that nothing in the world was so wholesome. She complained of the heat, gave advice to Mr Knightley's gardener, who was too polite to answer, and ate quite as many as she picked. Emma, who loved the fruit but disliked the company, took her portion in another part of the garden.

At noon Mr Knightley's servants spread a plain cold meal beneath the trees, with bread, cold meat, fruit and cool drinks, and the guests, who had worked up an appetite, sat down on benches and rugs. It was the simplest of entertainments, but it was done with such generous good sense that even Mrs Elton, who had hoped for donkeys, found nothing to criticise. The conversation was cheerful and easy, the shade was deliciously cool, and for an hour or so nobody had a single unkind word to say.

From the end of a long walk Emma looked down over the meadows to Abbey-Mill Farm, where the cows were grazing and the smoke rose peacefully from the chimney. She saw how comfortable and how sensible a home it was, and she thought of Robert Martin and of the letter she had made Harriet send, and a pang of guilt crossed her heart. It was not a comfortable moment, and she turned away from the view with a quick, restless movement, as though she could leave the thought behind.

Mr Woodhouse, who would not have dreamed of sitting outdoors on a summer day, was installed in a pleasant room beside a small fire. There he spent the whole afternoon turning over Mr Knightley's old engravings and describing them to anyone who came to see him, and he declared that it was the most comfortable visit he had ever paid. Mr Knightley, who had arranged everything, took the praise in silence, and Emma, who noticed the kindness behind it, was quietly moved.

Frank, who had promised to be early, arrived at Donwell long after the others, flushed and restless from the heat, and he leaped from his horse without his usual smile. Emma, who saw that he was in a strange mood, was surprised to be answered with a short remark and a frown when she asked about his journey. He wandered about the garden, ate nothing and spoke to no one for more than a minute.

Soon after his arrival, Frank announced that he could not endure the heat of the day any longer, and that he must go, and he mounted his horse and rode away much sooner than anyone had expected. Mr Weston, who was puzzled, could not understand what had come over his son, and Emma wondered whether the strain of his aunt's illness had affected him. Nobody present guessed the real cause of his restlessness, and the explanation was not to be discovered for some time to come.

Jane Fairfax, who had been unusually quiet all day, slipped away from the party in a hurry and set off alone along the hot road to Highbury, without waiting for anyone. Her friends begged her to rest, but she answered that she was only tired and would manage perfectly well. Mr Knightley, who had seen her face as she left, stood for a long moment looking after her.

Mr Weston, as the party sat on benches in the garden and watched the evening light, proposed an expedition to Box Hill. It was a famous hill with a lovely view, and the company agreed that it would be delightful, though Emma, who hoped Frank would join them, looked forward to it most. Mrs Elton, who had hoped to organise a picnic of her own, was consoled by being asked to help choose the day.

The party set out for Box Hill on a fine morning, in two carriages and on horseback, with baskets of food and the highest possible hopes for a delightful day. The roads wound through the green lanes of Surrey, past cornfields and hedges and quiet villages, and the guests were soon chattering with the cheerful excitement of children on a holiday. Only Jane Fairfax, seated in a corner, was unusually silent, and only Mr Knightley seemed to notice it.

The party reached Box Hill and sat down on the grass with their baskets, and the view across the valley was beautiful, but the day, from some unaccountable cause, was dull. The company broke into little groups that did not mix, conversation languished, and a sort of quarrelsome restlessness settled over everyone. Emma, who had expected so much, felt as if a cloud had passed over the sun, though there was not a cloud in the sky.

Frank, who had arrived in the highest spirits, talked loudly and gaily to Emma, flirting with her more openly than he had ever done before, and she, to her shame, answered in the same tone. Jane sat silent a little way off, and Mr Knightley, who was watching from beneath a tree, frowned in a manner that Emma noticed and did not like. She told herself that she was merely being agreeable, which is the excuse of every foolish girl.

Frank, by now almost feverish with spirits, raised his hand and commanded the attention of the whole party. He declared that Miss Woodhouse required everyone to say either one thing very clever, or two things moderately clever, or three things very dull indeed. Some of the party laughed at the notion, others looked unwilling, and Mr Knightley said nothing at all, for it seemed a harmless game and yet it was to be the cruellest hour of the summer.

Miss Bates, who sat with a basket on her lap and a look of simple good humour, cried that she would certainly manage the three dull things. She was sure, she said, to say three dull things as soon as she opened her mouth, and she laughed heartily at her own joke, never imagining that anyone could be unkind. In a lifetime of poverty and gossip she had hardly ever been treated with real unkindness, and the silence that followed was very slightly too long.

Emma, who was flushed with the heat and the nonsense and the excitement of Frank's attention, laughed and cried that Miss Bates might find some difficulty, because she would be limited to saying only three dull things at once. The words were light, and the laugh was careless, but their meaning was unmistakable, and the party fell silent with embarrassment. Several people looked away in confusion, and Mr Knightley, who had been watching her closely, turned a face of stone toward her.

Miss Bates understood at once, and a painful colour rose in her kind face, and she said, in a small, shaken voice, that she would certainly try to be quiet in future, since she knew that she talked too much. Emma, who saw how deeply the blow had gone home, felt a hot shame creep over her, but she was too proud and too confused to speak. The picnic, which had never been merry, ended soon afterwards in a general and uncomfortable silence, and everyone was glad to see the carriages.

As the party prepared to leave, Mr Knightley took Emma aside at the carriage door and, in a voice of low, steady disappointment, told her that she had been unfeeling and unworthy of herself. Miss Bates, he said, was poor, old, foolish and always kind, and to laugh at her in public was to forget everything that good breeding means. His words were quite just, and for that reason they stung more than any insult.

Emma wept all the way home in the carriage with her face turned toward the window, so that her friends should not see, and she was too unhappy even to wipe her eyes. She was bitterly ashamed that Mr Knightley, whose good opinion she valued above any other, had found her so unkind, and she felt it as the greatest grief of her life. The beautiful golden evening outside the carriage window, with its quiet fields and singing birds, seemed to her a cruel mockery.

That night Emma sat for a long time at her bedroom window, watching the dusk deepen over the empty road, and thinking of nothing but her own fault. She resolved that, as soon as it was light, she would go to see Miss Bates and make what amends she could, whatever it cost her pride. It was a small beginning, but it was the start of a real change in her.

The next morning Emma walked to the Bateses' house and sat beside Miss Bates in the little parlour, taking the old lady's hand with a gentleness that surprised them both. Miss Bates, who was incapable of bearing a grudge, received her with a warmth that was almost harder to endure than reproaches, and she talked cheerfully of the weather, of her mother and of Jane. Emma listened humbly and in silence, feeling with every sentence that she did not in the least deserve such kindness.

Miss Bates explained, with her usual flow of words, that Jane was unwell and lying down in her room, and that she could not see even the kindest visitor. Emma looked at the closed door of the inner room and felt a general atmosphere of trouble that no amount of chatter could cover. She went away uneasy, aware that she had never really understood the quiet girl on the other side of it.

As Emma left the Bateses' house she met Mr Knightley, who was riding out of Highbury on his way to London to stay with his brother, and she stopped him in the road. With her cheeks red and her eyes bright, she told him honestly that she knew she had been wrong and that she had come from Miss Bates. He looked at her searchingly, and the stern lines of his face began to relax.

Mr Knightley, convinced that her repentance was real, said with great kindness that he had never doubted her heart, and then, to her astonishment, he raised her hand to his lips and kissed it. He mounted his horse and rode away toward London, leaving Emma standing in the road with a warm and very peculiar feeling that she did not know how to name. It was, she decided after a moment's reflection, simply the great relief of being forgiven by someone whose good opinion mattered to her so much.

Jane Fairfax, pale and thin, sat at a window with a letter in her hands and told her aunt that she had made up her mind to be a governess. She could not bear, she said, to be a burden any longer, and when Emma called with offers of kindness, she thanked her politely and declined each of them in turn. It was clear that some great trouble was weighing on her, though no one could guess what it was.

Mrs Elton, bursting with importance, told the neighbours that she had found a most excellent situation for Jane with her friend Mrs Smallridge, who lived near Bristol and who had young children. To everybody's surprise Jane had accepted it, and she was to leave as soon as she could be spared. Miss Bates, who was proud and sad at the same time, could hardly speak of it without tears.

Emma heard that Jane was ill, and she sent a basket of the best arrowroot from the Hartfield store, which she hoped would tempt the poor girl's appetite. It came back within the hour with a message of thanks and a polite explanation that Miss Fairfax wanted nothing at all. Emma, who had never before been refused a kindness, did not at first know what to think.

Emma stared at the returned basket and understood that Jane, whose pride was as great as her own, did not want any favour from a girl who had never offered her real friendship. She saw, with a clearness that was painful, how coldly she had treated her neighbour for months, out of nothing but a dislike that she had never bothered to examine. Emma resolved to be a better friend, if the chance was ever given her.

Before long, a letter from Yorkshire announced that Mrs Churchill had died suddenly, and the whole of Highbury discussed the matter with a certain sombre decorum. It was observed, with a gravity that did not quite conceal curiosity, that the old lady's death had set her nephew free to do as he pleased. Emma, who had no clue yet to what lay beneath the surface, supposed only that it was a pity for his feelings.

Emma walked slowly through the Highbury street with her mind full of Frank, and she wondered what a young man would do when the power that governed his life was suddenly taken away. She thought of how his smile would look in black, of the grief that he must feel and of the hundred changes that freedom might bring. It never crossed her mind that the first change would be a wedding, and that it would not be hers.

Mrs Weston came to Hartfield with an open letter in her hand and a face that mingled apprehension and joy, and she asked Emma to listen quietly to what she had to say. Frank, she told her, had been engaged to Jane Fairfax in secret for many months, and they had kept the engagement hidden from everyone, even from his father. Emma, who thought for a moment that she must have misheard, could only sit and stare.

As the truth sank in, Emma went hot and cold by turns, for she remembered every careless word she had spoken to Frank about Jane. She recalled every foolish guess about Mr Dixon and the piano and every smiling remark about Jane's reserve, and she saw that Frank had listened to it all with a perfectly straight face. She did not know whether to be angry with him or with herself, and on the whole she decided that she was more angry with herself.

Mr Weston, found walking in the Randalls garden with an expression half smiling and half sad, told Emma that he had forgiven his son at once, and that the shock had been followed by a surprising gladness. Frank had known that his aunt, who despised any match not made for money, would never have consented, and so he had kept silent until her death. Mr Weston, who loved Jane's gentle character, said that he could hardly wish for a better daughter.

Emma took Frank's letter to the window and read it slowly and carefully, with a deepening frown. She learned that he had fallen in love with Jane Fairfax at Weymouth, where he had met her among the Campbells' party, and that the piano had been his secret gift. He wrote with humility and charm, begging pardon for his behaviour toward Emma herself and saying that his manner had been a mask, and Emma, who had been the mask, felt both hurt and, grudgingly, forgiving.

Emma paced the garden path at Hartfield with her hands clasped behind her, struggling with a new and painful thought. If Harriet had really placed her hopes on Frank, as Emma had so confidently supposed, then the poor girl was about to suffer a second disappointment, and once more it would be Emma's doing. She knew that she must tell Harriet at once, and as gently as she could.

Over tea at Randalls, Mrs Weston told Emma, with tears in her eyes, how much Jane had suffered from the secret, hiding her feelings through every public party and every curious conversation. The post-office walks, the pale face, the refused kindnesses and the sudden decision to become a governess all took on a new meaning. Emma saw that Frank's playful behaviour, for all its charm, had been very unkind to the girl he loved.

Emma held Harriet's hands beside the fire and told her, with the greatest tenderness, that Frank was engaged to Jane Fairfax and that all of Emma's hopes had been mistaken. To her astonishment, Harriet only smiled shyly and said that she had never cared for Frank in that way, and that her heart belonged to someone else. Emma, who had been preparing herself for tears and consolation, was for a moment quite struck dumb with surprise.

Harriet, her cheeks flushed and her eyes shining, spoke shyly of the night of the ball and of the shame that had threatened to overwhelm her. She spoke of the hand that had been held out in kindness when all the others had looked away, and she said that she had loved that man ever since. She would never have dared to dream of it, she added, if Emma had not taught her that a girl might look above her station, and Emma's heart gave a sudden lurch.

Harriet spoke the name of Mr Knightley, softly and with the trust of a child, and Emma rose without a word and walked out into the garden, with her hand pressed to her heart. In one blinding moment she understood the meaning of every jealous thought, every warm look and every quarrel of the past year, and she knew that she loved him herself, and had loved him for a long time. She had been so busy arranging other people's hearts that she had never once examined her own.

Emma sat motionless in her room as the night deepened, going over every hour she had spent with Mr Knightley and every sharp word she had said at the thought of his marrying anyone. She saw that her horror of the idea had been the cry of her own heart, and that her heart had been right. And now, by a bitter irony, it was her own protégée, the girl she had taught to look above her station, who might win him.

Emma sat at breakfast the next morning while her father spoke at length about the weather, and she answered him with her lips only, for her mind was far away. She knew her own heart now, and she felt sick with remorse that she had led poor Harriet toward a hope that could only end in sorrow. She was not certain which of the two of them was in the worse case.

Emma took out the old book of riddles and turned its pages slowly, and each one reminded her of some folly she had committed, from the charade of Mr Elton to the portrait of Harriet. She saw how her blind confidence in her own cleverness had injured the people she most wished to help. If only a single year could be unwritten, she thought, she would do everything differently.

Mr Knightley, who had read Mrs Weston's letter in London and imagined Emma's grief, came back at once and arrived at Hartfield with his horse splashed with mud and his face anxious. He had reasoned that she must be unhappy at Frank's engagement, and he had hurried away from his brother's house without waiting to finish his business. It was exactly the action of a man who cared more for a friend than for his own convenience.

Mr Knightley walked into the garden of Hartfield and found Emma by a gate, looking pale and thoughtful, and he took her hand and said that he had come to comfort her for the loss of Frank. Emma, flushing, replied with a kind of nervous haste that he need not trouble himself, because she had never been in love with Frank at all and had never been deceived on that score. It was the first plain truth that she had told in a long while.

Mr Knightley's whole face brightened at her words, and he admitted, with an odd laugh, that he had been jealous of Frank Churchill for a long time, though he had always known that he had no right to be. Emma could hardly breathe, and she turned her eyes to the gravel at her feet so that he should not read what was written on her face. They walked on a few steps in a silence so charged with feeling that neither of them dared to be the first to break it.

Walking slowly beside her under the trees, Mr Knightley said in a lower and more serious voice that he could not be only a friend to her any longer. He had, he added, a great deal to say, and Emma, who was quite sure that he was about to confess his love for Harriet, felt her heart sink like a stone. Her cheeks went pale, and she knew with perfect certainty that she could not bear to hear it.

Emma, who could not bear to hear what she expected, turned away and begged him to say nothing more, at least for a little while. Mr Knightley stopped, looking hurt, and said in a rough, unsteady voice that he could not make fine speeches, and that if he loved a woman less he might talk about it more easily. Emma, hearing these words, stood perfectly still, with a wild hope beginning to rise in her heart.

Then Mr Knightley took her hand, and in the quiet evening light he told her, in plain and honest words, that he had loved her for years. Nothing in the world, he said, would make him happier than to call her his wife, and Emma, scarcely believing her ears, answered with tears of joy that she had been as blind as a girl could be. She loved him, she said, with all her heart, and it was the happiest moment of her life.

Even in her happiness Emma remembered Harriet, and she confessed in great distress that her friend believed herself to be in love with him, and that she had been encouraged to do so. Mr Knightley listened with astonishment and real sorrow, for he had only meant to be kind at the ball, and he had never imagined that his courtesy could be taken for something more. They agreed, with perfect tenderness on both sides, that they must be very gentle with her and let her down as kindly as possible.

Emma looked through the window at her father sitting in his chair, and a shadow crossed her happiness, for she knew that she could never leave him alone in his old age. She told Mr Knightley so with tears in her eyes, but he thought for only a moment and then offered, with a generous smile, to move into Hartfield himself. It was the kind of solution that only love could have found, and Donwell, he said, would take care of itself.

Some days later Harriet received a second letter from Robert Martin, who had not stopped caring for her in all those months and who now asked again, with the same honest simplicity, whether she would be his wife. She read it with a happy blush, and, to everyone's relief, she accepted him gladly and at once. She had learned that a kind heart is worth more than a fine coat.

Emma threw her arms around Harriet in a sunlit room, with Mr Knightley smiling in the doorway, and she wished her joy with a warmth that brought tears to both of their eyes. She was delighted by Harriet's choice, and she saw clearly how foolish and how proud she had been to turn her friend away from so good a man. It was the happiest sort of repentance, the kind that is rewarded at once and far beyond anything that it deserves.

It was learned, at about this time, that Harriet's father was a respectable tradesman, an honest man with a comfortable income and no claim whatever to be a gentleman. Emma, who had been so sure for so long that her friend's birth must be grand, laughed aloud at her old romantic notions, and Mr Knightley joined her. She admitted that she would never again judge a person's worth by guesswork about who their parents were.

Mr Woodhouse, hearing that his daughter was to be married, sat worried in his armchair and said that he did not like any change, and that she had better not go. Emma and Mr Knightley talked to him patiently, explaining that nothing need change very much, since Mr Knightley would live at Hartfield. His objections went on until, one night, thieves robbed a neighbour's hen house, and he began to feel that it would be very comfortable to have a man in the house.

Frank came back to Highbury at last, looking years older and a great deal happier, and he found Emma in the garden at Hartfield and held out his hand with an anxious smile. Emma, who had every reason to be angry with him, found that she could not be, and she shook his hand with a laugh and wished him joy. She had begun to see that two people in love can behave very foolishly, and that she was hardly the one to complain.

Emma sat at her desk and wrote to Jane a long, warm letter of congratulation, in which she begged forgiveness for every coldness and stupidity of the past year. Jane answered with a kindness that touched Emma deeply, and the two young women, who had never been friends, discovered that they could be. It was only a pity, Emma thought, that they had wasted so much time.

On a bright autumn morning Emma and Mr Knightley were married in the church at Highbury, with only their closest friends beside them and no more show than good taste required. The bride was calm, the bridegroom was grave and happy, and Mr Woodhouse, who had made up his mind to be brave, cried only a very little. Nobody who watched them walk out into the sunshine could doubt that this was one match which no one had arranged.

Mrs Elton, who had observed the wedding from a window of the vicarage with a critical eye, declared to her husband that she had never seen anything so mean and so quiet. There was hardly any lace, she said, no grand carriage and a mere handful of guests, and she had been told that Emma was to marry a man of fortune. She could only suppose, she added, that the fortune had been mislaid, and Mr Elton, who had learned to say yes to his wife on every occasion, said yes.

At the wedding breakfast Mr Woodhouse, who had been studying the wedding cake with deep suspicion for a quarter of an hour, announced to the company that a very small piece could do no harm to anybody. Mr Perry, who had been consulted in advance, solemnly agreed, and the old gentleman, to everyone's delight, was seen to eat the crumbs with every sign of pleasure. He told his new son-in-law that he had never believed that he was losing a daughter at all.

Emma and Mr Knightley settled at Hartfield, and in their company Mr Woodhouse lived comfortably for several more years. Harriet married Robert Martin soon afterward, and the friends met often, and Emma now left the matchmaking to other people. She had found, to her real surprise, that the happiest match of all had been waiting for her in a neighbour's house.
